We enjoy solving complex problems through creativity, critical thinking, and collaboration. We are looking for enthusiastic members skilled in programming, AI/ML, web development, UI/UX, data science, astronomy, or research. summary:
SARScope is an interactive, open-source web application that makes Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data easier to understand and explore. Built for the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge, it uses a simple drag to reveal slider to show how Earth's surface changes over time, from earthquake damage and glacier retreat to land subsidence.

Users can explore real world examples along with their locations, observation dates, and explanations of what causes these changes. The goal is to make complex radar imagery understandable not just to scientists, but also to students, researchers, and the general public.

SARScope is also designed with future NASA-ISRO NISAR data in mind. Its data layer can be connected to the ASF API when NISAR data becomes available, allowing the application to move beyond sample imagery and support real-world observations without redesigning the interface.
details:
# What it does and how it works

SARScope is a web-based tool that helps people explore and understand Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery without needing an extensive background in remote sensing. It uses a simple drag-to-reveal slider to compare two radar images of the same location taken at different times. By moving the slider, users can see changes in the landscape, such as ground movement after an earthquake, glacier retreat, or land subsidence.

Each example also includes its location, acquisition dates, and a short explanation of the science behind the imagery. This introduces concepts such as surface roughness, dielectric properties, and radar phase in a way that is easier to follow. The aim is to help users understand not just what changed, but also how radar helps us observe those changes.

# Benefits and Intended Impact

SAR data is widely used in Earth observation, but interpreting it can be difficult for people who are unfamiliar with radar imagery. SARScope aims to make this information easier to access and understand.

Students and educators can use it as a learning resource, researchers can use it to introduce SAR concepts, and people interested in environmental changes can explore real examples from different parts of the world. It could also help local planners and disaster-response teams gain a clearer visual understanding of surface changes, although it is intended as an educational and exploratory tool rather than a replacement for professional monitoring systems.

By presenting radar imagery alongside simple explanations and real-world examples, SARScope makes satellite observations more approachable and useful to a wider audience.

# Tools and Technologies

The application is being developed using React with TypeScript and Vite. Tailwind CSS handles the styling, while Framer Motion supports the drag-to-reveal interaction. The application is deployed on Vercel.

We are keeping the data layer separate from the user interface so that different SAR data sources can be integrated without rebuilding the application. The initial version uses pre-processed Sentinel-1 C-band and UAVSAR imagery. This provides a practical way to demonstrate the concept using existing datasets.

The architecture is also designed with NASA-ISRO NISAR data in mind. Once suitable NISAR products are accessible through the ASF API, they can be integrated into the existing data layer, subject to data availability, format compatibility, and processing requirements.

# Creativity and Team Considerations

For the interface, we chose a scientific editorial design inspired by research publications and scientific instruments. It uses a paper-and-ink colour palette, straightforward typography, and a minimal layout to keep attention on the imagery and the information being presented. We deliberately avoided the usual dark, dashboard-heavy aesthetic in favour of something that feels approachable and easy to navigate.

An important consideration during development was the availability of NISAR data. Since the mission is still in its early operational and calibration phase, building the entire application around live NISAR data would not be practical. Instead, we chose Sentinel-1 and UAVSAR datasets to make the prototype usable with existing imagery while keeping the system ready for future NISAR integration.

Our focus is to build something that works with available data today, explains the science clearly, and can grow as new satellite datasets become accessible.
